CausalChain: Chronic inflammation/cholestasis -> recruitment/activation of CAFs -> secretion of exosomes containing TGFβ and other bioactive molecules -> induction of epigenetic modifications (e.g., DNA hypermethylation) in cholangiocarcinoma cells -> synergy with IDH mutation-driven accumulation of 2-hydroxyglutarate -> enhancement of EMT and cancer stem cell properties -> increased chemoresistance
Hypothesis: In cholangiocarcinoma, CAF-derived exosomes mediate epigenetic reprogramming that, particularly in the context of IDH mutations, drives EMT and chemoresistance; inhibition of CAF-derived exosome release may re-sensitize tumors to chemotherapy.
Abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is marked by extensive heterogeneity, wherein interactions between tumor cells and the microenvironment play a pivotal role in disease progression and treatment resistance. We propose that cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs) secrete exosomes that carry bioactive molecules capable of modulating the epigenetic landscape of neighboring cholangiocarcinoma cells. In particular, this mechanism may synergize with intrinsic mutations—such as those in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)—to amplify oncometabolite-driven DNA hypermethylation, promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and increase cancer stem cell traits, collectively contributing to chemoresistance. Targeting CAF-derived exosomal signaling might therefore restore drug sensitivity and improve therapeutic outcomes in CCA.
